📣 We're #hiring: Analyst, Loss of Control Incidents (contract) 

The Loss of Control Observatory at CLTR is a world-first effort to detect and monitor misaligned, uncontrolled AI systems in the wild. Our pilot, backed by the UK AI Security Institute, picked up a fivefold rise in reported loss of control incidents this year and drew international news coverage. We're now scaling it into a robust platform, and we need someone to turn its data into analysis that governments and AI developers can trust and act on.

You'll own a monthly insight report and ad hoc Substack pieces on notable incidents, with scope to lead one or two major reports a year. You'll also help shape where the Observatory goes next, from new data sources to changes in how we classify incidents.

We're looking for someone who:
➡️ Knows the loss of control landscape well, whether through AI safety research or a threat assessment or intelligence background
➡️ Writes clearly and concisely for expert and policy readers
➡️ Handles aggregate data with care and can tell a real trend from a detection artefact (no coding required)
➡️ Works independently and delivers to a monthly rhythm

We'd especially love to hear from people who have written analytical products for government or national security readers, and from quantitative or social science researchers who want their work to reach decision-makers.

📅 6-month contract, around 2 days a week, with possible extension
 💷 £600–£800/day, plus a supplement of up to £300 per day for senior specialists
 📍 UK-based, with our Westminster office available (remote considered in some cases)
 ⏰ Apply by 9am, Monday 19 October – full details in the comments below

When does onboarding actually start at your company? With the offer, the signed contract, or the moment a candidate looks promising?

That sounds like a small detail, but it decides whether your hiring-to-onboarding handoff works or quietly creates problems. If onboarding tasks start from a recruiting milestone, unapproved candidates can end up with access requests, equipment orders and welcome emails. If they start from a copied checklist, someone retypes details and gets the start date wrong.

A cleaner way to build the handoff:

1. Start from the approved hire, not the assessment.
 Define a release gate in plain words: HR approves the hire, confirms the required details, and checks that no employee record already exists. If any of those is unresolved, the handoff stays pending and goes to a named owner instead of generating downstream work.

2. Transfer a small, verified set of fields.
 Name, contact email, role, manager, start date and work arrangement are a good starting list. Interview notes, assessments and hiring deliberations should not travel into general onboarding tasks. Ask of every field: which onboarding action depends on it? If none does, leave it out.

3. Give every task a person, a deadline and proof of completion.
 Group the work into HR preparation, manager preparation, access preparation and first-day confirmation. A submitted access request isn't working access, and a calendar invite isn't a first-day plan.

4. Test the failures, not just the success.
 Run one complete test hire and one incomplete one. Submit the same approved handoff twice. Change the start date. The incomplete one should stop, the duplicate should be recognised, and the new date shouldn't leave old deadlines behind.

5. Handle changes as a review, not a restart.
 When a start date or manager changes, update the existing record and its affected tasks. Don't rerun the whole new-hire sequence.

This is where HRSpace makes life easier. AI recruitment, onboarding and HR workflows sit in one cloud platform, alongside time-off, reviews and an internal service desk, so the handoff happens inside one system instead of between two. It doesn't replace your approval rules, and which steps are automatic depends on how your account is configured, so test your own sequence before using it for live hires.

You can read the complete workflow on our website, including the pre-start checklist, the validation steps and a troubleshooting section for the most common problems. [ https://lnkd.in/dbpyfn_S ]

The customer said "we need the integration by March."
 
The engineering team said "we need 3 more hires by January."
 
The recruiter said "I can have candidates in 6 to 8 weeks."
 
That math does not work. And every founder selling into enterprise knows it.
 
Enterprise deals have a rhythm that does not care about your hiring timeline. The procurement team sets a deadline. The security review has a window. The budget approval expires at end of quarter. Miss any of those, and the deal dies quietly. Not because your product failed. Because your team could not move fast enough.
 
I watched a compliance-focused AI startup lose a $400K contract last quarter. Their product worked. The pilot passed. The customer was ready to sign. But the integration needed custom engineering the team did not have bandwidth for. By the time they found a contractor, the procurement window closed. The customer went with a competitor who shipped the integration in 3 weeks.
 
The product was better. The engineering capacity was worse. The competitor won.
 
If you are selling AI into healthcare, insurance, financial services, or anything regulated, your engineering team's capacity is not a hiring problem. It is a sales problem.
 
Every week your integration sits unbuilt is a week your champion inside the enterprise account loses leverage. Their boss starts asking why this is taking so long. The internal sponsor starts hedging. The deal slips from this quarter to next quarter to "let's revisit."
 
The founders closing enterprise deals fastest right now have one thing in common: they decoupled engineering capacity from the hiring cycle.

I have seen the underbelly of agency SMM: businesses pay for the illusion of marketing, not marketing itself.
   *   In the B2B segment, expertise is merely a baseline requirement. No one signs a contract worth tens of thousands of dollars just because you know how to do your job. 

When dozens of companies offer similar services, a business inevitably falls into the Commodity Trap. 
    *  The only way to escape price dumping and build a personal monopoly is to become a "trusted insider" for the client. People hire someone whose views, methodology, and values resonate with them and make sense. 

But how do you speak the same language as your clients? 

Most assembly-line agencies respond to this with cookie-cutter actions: they generate generic target audience personas using AI, overlay superficial pain points, and churn out banal posts.

In complex niches, this does not work. 

Real decision-makers (CEOs, CFOs, managing partners) suffer from a "public restraint syndrome." They rarely write their own posts in the public feed due to compliance, NDAs, or a basic lack of time. If you try to analyze them based on their personal publications, their profiles will seem empty.

However, their digital footprint never disappears: 
1.	They ask unvalidated, raw questions in closed groups and specialized chats, discussing the actual mess in their business processes.
 2.	They debate under posts by industry leaders, defending their approaches to hiring, deal structuring, or compliance. 
3.	They use precise internal industry phrasing without the glossy marketing fluff.
When content addresses the exact unresolved questions that industry key players were arguing about in the comments yesterday, it creates an effect of absolute resonance. 
     The client sees a like-minded peer who understands the context of their challenges deeper than anyone else. And at that exact moment, the price issue ceases to be a dealbreaker.

💸 The Shortcut Tax: €825M.

That's what the Dutch data protection authority fined Uber in August for letting software deactivate driver accounts without meaningful human review.

Picture the office badge reader firing someone because they swiped in late three times. Efficient. Under GDPR Article 22, also not allowed when the decision has a serious effect on a person, like cutting off their income.

The regulator also found drivers weren't properly told how those automated decisions worked. Uber disagrees and says it will appeal, so this isn't the last word. The lesson for in-house counsel holds either way.

If I were walking a leadership team through this, I'd start with one AI governance question: where does a system make a call about a person with no human able to change the outcome?

🛠️ The cheaper fix:
      → Map those decisions: account suspensions, fraud flags, hiring screens, pricing or credit calls.
      → Put a reviewer in the loop with the authority and the information to overrule the system, not just click "approve."
      → Tell people when it happens and give them a real way to contest it.

For most companies, the biggest AI risk right now isn’t a missed opportunity. It’s liability exposure — and the cases are already piling up.

A few cases every director should know:

– Mata v. Avianca (2023): lawyers sanctioned for filing a brief that cited court decisions ChatGPT had invented.

– Deloitte Australia (2025): part of a A$440,000 government contract refunded after the report was found to contain a fabricated court quote and references to research that doesn’t exist.

– EEOC v. iTutorGroup (2023): $365,000 settlement after hiring software automatically rejected older applicants.

– Moffatt v. Air Canada (2024): the airline held to a refund policy its website chatbot made up.

– SEC (2024): two investment advisers paid $400,000 combined for overstating their use of AI.

And lawsuits still working through the courts allege AI-driven harm in hiring screens (Mobley v. Workday) and in health-coverage denials (the UnitedHealth nH Predict case).

Notice what these have in common: none of them required a bad AI strategy. Each required an AI output that nobody qualified checked before it reached a court, a client, a customer, or an applicant.

That’s the exposure most boards haven’t mapped yet: AI already inside the company, used in consequential work, with no one accountable for the result.
